title: Body, soul, mind
hookLine: the body senses, the soul desires, the mind rules (Meditations 3.16)

lines: A CHARIOT, A DRIVER, TWO HORSES.
cards: Plato pictured the soul as a chariot: a driver and two winged horses, one pulling well and one pulling wild. Marcus Aurelius, closing his third book, offers a plainer picture, with no horses at all.

A person, he says, is three things: a body, a soul, and a mind, each with its own job. Then a harder question: which of those jobs belongs to the good person alone? His answer takes a surprising route.

teach.b: To the body, Marcus writes, belong the senses. To the soul, which for him means the life force that wants and moves, belong the impulses. To the mind belong the principles.
Then he checks each job against who else has it. Receiving impressions through the senses?

teach.h: CATTLE, BEASTS AND TRAITORS SHARE THEM.
teach.b: Cattle do that. Being yanked around by desire? Wild animals do that, he says, and so did tyrants like Phalaris and Nero.
Even using the mind to pursue what seems useful? People who betray their country and do anything behind closed doors do that too. None of the three, by itself, makes a good person.
So what belongs to the good person alone?

To welcome what happens and what's woven for them; to keep the spirit within untroubled, undisturbed by a crowd of impressions; to follow it quietly, as a god; never to say anything false or do anything unjust.
This isn't contempt for the body. Marcus is sorting jobs, not condemning them.
His point is about who drives. Senses report. Desires pull.
Principles decide. When the order flips, and the pull decides, things go badly.
That closes book three. It began with time running short, and it ends with the one thing worth spending that time on: a mind that keeps its own counsel, honestly, whatever comes.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes use Meditations 3.16 as a quick check-in: what the body senses, what the soul wants, and which principle the mind will steer by.

o: the only part of you that truly matters to Marcus
the part of you that wants, and must be made to obey
the part of you that senses, in Marcus's three parts

s: Marcus says the body and desire are evil
he's sorting what each part does; his point is about which part steers.
Marcus says even traitors use the mind to pursue what seems useful
so the mind's cleverness alone doesn't make a good person.
book three ends here, before the fire of book four.

games.q: you're tired, a craving is pulling hard, and your mind already knows what it wants to do. who gets the reins, in 3.16?
o: the impulse: it's strongest right now.
the mind, steering by a principle.
games.why: Marcus: senses report, impulses pull, principles decide. the good person's part is letting the mind drive.

practice: Check in with each of the three: first the body, what are your senses reporting, warmth, an ache, the sound in the room? Then the part that wants: what's pulling at you right now, food, your phone, a worry, a person?
Then the mind: choose one principle to steer by for the next hour, and let it take the reins, gently.

wordCard.voice: Body, soul, mind. Marcus says the body senses, the soul desires, the mind holds principles, and the good person lets the mind steer. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: body, soul, mind, the three parts Marcus names in 3.16.

carryVoice: Your line: three parts. Senses report, desires pull, principles decide who drives. Book three, done.
